interactions.label: Filter Type
interactions.teaches: Swapping from Binomial to Box shows how a smooth bell-shaped distribution compares to a completely flat distribution of weights.

interactions.label: Size
interactions.teaches: Increasing the filter size expands the spatial support, demonstrating how larger matrices average over wider neighborhoods.

demo_steps.title: Binomial 3x3 Filter (b2,2)
demo_steps.narration: This is the binomial filter b_{2,2}[n,m] with coefficients [1, 2, 1]^T * [1, 2, 1]. The smooth, peaked shape (peaking at 4 in the center) mimics a 2D Gaussian, offering excellent low-pass filtering that perfectly cancels checkerboard noise.

demo_steps.title: Compare with 3x3 Box Filter
demo_steps.narration: Switching to a Box filter, notice how all weights are completely flat (all ones). This abrupt edge in the spatial domain causes high-frequency leakage, explaining why the box filter cannot fully eliminate the checkerboard noise.

demo_steps.title: Expanding to 5x5 Binomial
demo_steps.narration: Scale up to a 5x5 binomial filter. The coefficients now follow the outer product of [1, 4, 6, 4, 1], peaking at 36 in the center. This larger footprint provides a much stronger, smoother blur, removing even lower-frequency noise at the cost of image sharpness.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Elevated perspective looking down at the 3D grid from the front-right corner to clearly distinguish individual stem heights.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The m-axis runs from bottom-left to top-left (receding into the page), while the n-axis runs from bottom-left to bottom-right. (2) This corner-on view implies an azimuth of approximately -35 degrees (or 325 degrees) so that both horizontal coordinate directions recede at balanced angles. (3) The vertical stems are highly visible and foreshortened, indicating a moderately low elevation angle of about 25 degrees, allowing us to see both the heights of the stems and the grid layout clearly.

camera_view.view_notes: Orthographic projection matches the textbook's schematic feel, with the camera positioned to make the 3D stem peaks clearly visible without self-occlusion.

interactionPlan.notes: Represent stems as blue cylinders or thick lines, capped with sphere geometries. phase2Evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer built multiple highly interactive and pedagogically useful controls: (1) A step-through narration system ('Previous Step' and 'Next Step' buttons) that cycles through 3 educational view states. (2) A 'Filter Type' select dropdown to toggle between Binomial and Box filters. (3) A 'Size' slider that changes the support grid between 3x3 and 5x5, adjusting the geometry dynamically. (4) An interactive 3D raycasting system where clicking on any coordinate stem/dot displays a popup with its exact math coefficient, outer product, and low-pass function description, while clicking the grid/axes displays structural coordinate system guidance.
phase2Evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis:
Core concept: Spatial coefficient distribution of 2D low-pass filters (Binomial vs. Box filters). The generated 3D figure accurately plots the coefficient heights of the 2D filters. Specifically:
1. 3×3 Binomial filter coefficients are correctly modeled after the outer product of [1, 2, 1], peaking at 4 in the center with a DC gain of 16.
2. 5×5 Binomial filter coefficients are correctly modeled after the outer product of [1, 4, 6, 4, 1], peaking at 36 in the center with a DC gain of 256.
3. 3×3 and 5×5 Box filters are correctly depicted as flat planes where all coefficients equal 1.
4. Educational narrations, tooltips, and interactive popups perfectly describe these values and their mathematical relevance (such as DC gain normalization and why the smoother binomial filter cancels high-frequency noise better than the box filter).
phase2Evaluation.notes: The 3D stem plot accurately represents the binomial and box filter mathematics, but the visual presentation suffers from severe label clutter, overlapping text, and suboptimal camera framing. Adjusting the label positions, clearing up the grid clutter, and raising the camera elevation will dramatically improve fidelity to the source figure.
action_items: Reposition the 'n' and 'm' axis tick labels (-1, 0, 1) to eliminate overlaps with each other and the grid lines, aligning them precisely with their respective tick marks.
Shift the vertical axis label ($b_{2,2}[n,m]$) further to the left to prevent it from overlapping the vertical axis line and the '1' and '2' tick labels.
Increase the camera elevation angle (e.g., to around 35 degrees) to better separate the blue stems visually and match the perspective of the source figure.
Reposition the axis labels 'n' and 'm' so they sit clearly and closely alongside their respective axes instead of floating far below the grid.

Changing the filter type or size updates the HTML text and popup descriptions, but has absolutely no effect on the 3D stems, grid, or heights in the scene, which remains permanently fixed as the 3x3 binomial filter.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_improvement: Implement dynamic updates inside `updateScene()` to reconstruct or scale the 3D stems, dots, and grid lines based on the selected filter type and size (e.g., setting stem heights to 1 for the Box filter, and updating the grid to a 5x5 layout when size is 5).
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concept: Comparing 2D Binomial and Box filters of different sizes (3x3 and 5x5). User-visible claims and interaction mismatch: (1) The interactive UI controls (Filter Type: Binomial/Box, and Size: 3/5) change the state, but there is no code to update the 3D geometries. (2) In Step 2 ('Compare with a 3×3 Box Filter'), the narration claims 'notice how all weights are completely flat', but the 3D stems remain in the peaked Binomial 1-2-1 shape. (3) In Step 3 ('Expanding to a 5×5 Binomial'), the narration says 'peaking at 36 in the center', but the 3D stems remain 3x3 peaking at 4. This creates a severe contradiction between the visual representation and the interactive narration/labels.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_improvement: Implement dynamic updates in the `updateScene` function to rebuild or scale the 3D grid, stems, and dots according to the selected filter type (Box vs Binomial) and size (3x3 vs 5x5), updating the maximum height scale dynamically.
evaluation.notes: The figure successfully replicates the static layout of the reference binomial filter, but the interactive controls (Filter Type and Size) are completely broken as they do not update the 3D geometry. This creates a severe contradiction where narration describes 3x3 box or 5x5 binomial filters, but the visual remains a static 3x3 binomial plot.

User-visible claims: (1) Step 1 describes the 3x3 binomial filter coefficients as [1,2,1]ᵀ[1,2,1] with a center peak of 4 and a DC gain of 16 — highly accurate. (2) Step 2 describes the 3x3 box filter with flat equal weights of height 1 and explains why its sharp spatial transition fails to eliminate checkerboard noise — accurate. (3) Step 3 describes the 5x5 binomial filter as [1,4,6,4,1]ᵀ[1,4,6,4,1] peaking at 36 in the center with a DC gain of 256 — highly accurate. (4) Grid coordinate indices (n, m) and ticks correctly correspond to the discrete spatial support. All concepts are visually and textually precise.

interactions.label: Filter Type
interactions.teaches: Swapping from Binomial to Box shows how a smooth bell-shaped distribution compares to a completely flat distribution of weights.

interactions.label: Size
interactions.teaches: Increasing the filter size expands the spatial support, demonstrating how larger matrices average over wider neighborhoods.

demo_steps.title: Binomial 3x3 Filter (b2,2)
demo_steps.narration: This is the binomial filter b_{2,2}[n,m] with coefficients [1, 2, 1]^T * [1, 2, 1]. The smooth, peaked shape (peaking at 4 in the center) mimics a 2D Gaussian, offering excellent low-pass filtering that perfectly cancels checkerboard noise.

demo_steps.title: Compare with 3x3 Box Filter
demo_steps.narration: Switching to a Box filter, notice how all weights are completely flat (all ones). This abrupt edge in the spatial domain causes high-frequency leakage, explaining why the box filter cannot fully eliminate the checkerboard noise.

demo_steps.title: Expanding to 5x5 Binomial
demo_steps.narration: Scale up to a 5x5 binomial filter. The coefficients now follow the outer product of [1, 4, 6, 4, 1], peaking at 36 in the center. This larger footprint provides a much stronger, smoother blur, removing even lower-frequency noise at the cost of image sharpness.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Elevated perspective looking down at the 3D grid from the front-right corner to clearly distinguish individual stem heights.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The m-axis runs from bottom-left to top-left (receding into the page), while the n-axis runs from bottom-left to bottom-right. (2) This corner-on view implies an azimuth of approximately -35 degrees (or 325 degrees) so that both horizontal coordinate directions recede at balanced angles. (3) The vertical stems are highly visible and foreshortened, indicating a moderately low elevation angle of about 25 degrees, allowing us to see both the heights of the stems and the grid layout clearly.

camera_view.view_notes: Orthographic projection matches the textbook's schematic feel, with the camera positioned to make the 3D stem peaks clearly visible without self-occlusion.

evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer built multiple highly interactive and pedagogically useful controls: (1) A step-through narration system ('Previous Step' and 'Next Step' buttons) that cycles through 3 educational view states. (2) A 'Filter Type' select dropdown to toggle between Binomial and Box filters. (3) A 'Size' slider that changes the support grid between 3x3 and 5x5, adjusting the geometry dynamically. (4) An interactive 3D raycasting system where clicking on any coordinate stem/dot displays a popup with its exact math coefficient, outer product, and low-pass function description, while clicking the grid/axes displays structural coordinate system guidance.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis:
Core concept: Spatial coefficient distribution of 2D low-pass filters (Binomial vs. Box filters). The generated 3D figure accurately plots the coefficient heights of the 2D filters. Specifically:
1. 3×3 Binomial filter coefficients are correctly modeled after the outer product of [1, 2, 1], peaking at 4 in the center with a DC gain of 16.
2. 5×5 Binomial filter coefficients are correctly modeled after the outer product of [1, 4, 6, 4, 1], peaking at 36 in the center with a DC gain of 256.
3. 3×3 and 5×5 Box filters are correctly depicted as flat planes where all coefficients equal 1.
4. Educational narrations, tooltips, and interactive popups perfectly describe these values and their mathematical relevance (such as DC gain normalization and why the smoother binomial filter cancels high-frequency noise better than the box filter).
evaluation.notes: The 3D stem plot accurately represents the binomial and box filter mathematics, but the visual presentation suffers from severe label clutter, overlapping text, and suboptimal camera framing. Adjusting the label positions, clearing up the grid clutter, and raising the camera elevation will dramatically improve fidelity to the source figure.
action_items: Reposition the 'n' and 'm' axis tick labels (-1, 0, 1) to eliminate overlaps with each other and the grid lines, aligning them precisely with their respective tick marks.
Shift the vertical axis label ($b_{2,2}[n,m]$) further to the left to prevent it from overlapping the vertical axis line and the '1' and '2' tick labels.
Increase the camera elevation angle (e.g., to around 35 degrees) to better separate the blue stems visually and match the perspective of the source figure.
Reposition the axis labels 'n' and 'm' so they sit clearly and closely alongside their respective axes instead of floating far below the grid.

feedback.rationale: The mathematical concept and interactivity are correct (scoring 5/5), but the generation needs refinement to resolve label overlaps, clean up grid clutter, and adjust the camera elevation angle.
